title: Deals, Lesson 6: The fairness opinion and the board's duties
subtitle: Who protects minority shareholders, what the investment bank actually signs, and why the conflict is structural
whyItMatters: The seller's board decides on behalf of thousands of shareholders with no voice in the negotiation. A fairness opinion is the formal tool for showing they discharged that duty - and understanding the tool's limits matters as much as understanding the tool.
openingQuestion: What does a fairness opinion issued by an investment bank assert?
openingOptions: That this is the best price obtainable in the market
That the price falls within a range that is financially reasonable
That the deal will benefit both sides
That the target has been fully due-diligenced
explanation: This is a document routinely read as saying more than it does. It does not say the price is the best available, does not say the deal should be done, and does not substitute for due diligence. It asserts one narrow thing: that from a financial point of view, this price falls within a reasonable range for shareholders at the date of issue, on the valuation methods and assumptions set out in the document itself. Its legal value lies in showing the board took independent advice before deciding.

diagram.label: The board decides on shareholders' behalf
An adviser is engaged to give an independent opinion
The opinion: is the price within a reasonable range

realWorldExample.company: The conflict built into how advisers are paid
realWorldExample.description: An investment bank advising the seller usually takes a success fee - payable only if the deal completes, and scaled to deal value. If that same bank also issues the fairness opinion, it is being paid for the deal to happen while simultaneously being asked to judge objectively whether the price is fair. Good practice is to engage a different firm to issue the opinion on a fixed fee independent of the outcome. In shareholder litigation, the fee arrangement is among the first things challenged.

quiz.question: What is the seller's board's principal duty in a deal?
options: Preserving every employee's job for at least three years afterwards
Ensuring the deal completes on the timetable promised to the buyer in the heads of terms
Acting in shareholders' best interests, even where that differs from their own
Choosing the financially strongest bidder among those submitting valid offers
quiz.explanation: The second half is the important part: management may lose their jobs, or conversely gain a great deal from the deal, and this duty exists precisely because of those conflicts.

quiz.question: Why is the fairness opinion usually commissioned from a firm other than the deal adviser?
options: Because engaging two firms usually costs less than giving everything to one
Because regulators prohibit one firm from both advising and issuing the opinion
Because issuing the opinion needs a separate licence investment banks do not hold
Because the deal adviser takes a success fee and so has a financial interest in completion
quiz.explanation: This is a structural conflict rather than a matter of individual ethics, so the remedy has to be structural too: separate the roles and pay a fixed fee.

quiz.question: What does a no-shop clause in the agreement do?
options: Stops the seller actively seeking other buyers once signed with the current one
Stops the buyer approaching the seller's key staff before completion
Stops both sides disclosing the deal externally before the announcement date
Stops the seller's shareholders transferring shares between signing and closing
quiz.explanation: The clause usually comes with a carve-out letting the board consider a superior proposal if another party approaches unprompted - precisely because a duty to shareholders cannot be contracted away entirely.

quiz.question: What is the most important limitation of a fairness opinion?
options: It is valid only for thirty days from the date the adviser formally issues it
It assesses the price at one moment and does not assert this is the best option
It may not be used as evidence in litigation arising after the deal
It applies only to deals above a certain value threshold under current rules
quiz.explanation: A price can be both within a reasonable range and below what a more competitive sale process would have achieved. This document does not answer the second question.

quiz.question: Does holding a fairness opinion protect the board from a shareholder claim?
options: Yes, because responsibility transfers to the firm issuing the opinion
Yes, provided the opinion was issued before the board formally voted
No, it is evidence of a careful process rather than a shield
No, because shareholders cannot challenge board decisions at all
quiz.explanation: The board's duty of care remains the board's - a single document cannot buy it out. What is examined is the whole process: was the business shopped to others, were the adviser's conflicts handled, were alternatives to this deal considered. The fairness opinion is one link in that chain.

keyTakeaways: A fairness opinion says only that the price is within a reasonable range at one moment, not that it is the best price
The board owes a duty to shareholders even where it runs against its own interests
A success fee creates a structural conflict: separate the opinion role and pay a fixed fee
A no-shop clause usually carries a carve-out for a superior unsolicited proposal
A fair price and the best price are two different questions - this document answers only the first

practicePrompt.question: The board accepts the first offer it receives, supported by a fairness opinion. Shareholders sue on the basis that the business was never shopped competitively. Does the opinion protect the board?
options: Yes, because an independent firm confirmed the price was fair
Not really: it shows the price was reasonable, not the best available
No, because a fairness opinion has no legal weight at all
Yes, if issued by a firm taking no success fee
practicePrompt.explanation: This is the most commonly confused boundary in the whole lesson. A fairness opinion speaks to the outcome - the price. The shareholders' complaint here speaks to the process - whether the board did enough to find a better price. The two are judged separately, and a supportive opinion does not automatically answer the process question.

summary.keyIdea: A fairness opinion assesses the price, not the quality of the process that arrived at it
summary.commonMistake: Reading the opinion as an assertion that the deal is the best available option for shareholders
summary.action: Find the fairness opinion section in a shareholder circular and read the limitations paragraph carefully.

application.title: What to do
application.message: Open the shareholder circular for an announced deal. Find the section describing the fairness opinion and answer three questions: which firm issued it, how they were paid, and what limitations the document places on its own conclusion.
application.secondary: The limitations section is usually longer than the conclusion, and it tells you exactly what the document does not assert.

sections.text: This stage closes on the least technical question and the one with the most real consequences: who is responsible when a deal is agreed, and what they rely on when they sign.
Two different questions, and one document that answers only one

left.label: The question about price
left.text: Does this price fall within a range that is reasonable from a financial point of view. This is the question a fairness opinion answers, using the valuation methods covered in the valuation section.

right.label: The question about process
right.text: Did the board do enough to find the best available option: was there a competitive sale, were conflicts of interest handled, were other proposals considered. The other document does not answer this.

sections.title: The mechanisms protecting minority shareholders
sections.subtitle: None is sufficient alone; they compensate for each other

concepts.def: Confirms the price falls within a reasonable range. Strongest when issued by a firm taking no success fee.
Made up of directors with no interest in the deal, negotiating on behalf of the whole board. Most important where management is also the buyer.
Large deals must be approved by the shareholders in general meeting. This is the final mechanism, and the reason the circular sent to shareholders has to be complete.

sections.label: When management sits on both sides
sections.text: The hardest case is where management itself takes part in buying the company it runs. They know the true value better than anyone and have a direct interest in buying cheaply. Here a fairness opinion is not enough: practice requires an independent committee with power to engage its own advisers and to refuse the deal, together with the interested parties being excluded from the vote.

lines: A document confirming the price is fair does not replace a process that went looking for a better one.
This stage closes the deal mechanics: from the first EPS calculation to the final signature.
